summaries.example: Imagine a story about a talking backpack that travels to the moon. You know there is no such backpack, but you can still imagine its trip and feel excited when it gets home. The story gives you a game of make-believe. It may also include real facts, such as the moon being far from Earth.
summaries.summary: Fiction is a major part of human culture. We tell stories, watch films, look at pictures, and imagine what happens to characters. Philosophers ask what separates fiction from non-fiction. One idea says fiction is made by inventing stories. Another says a writer pretends to make ordinary claims, while readers understand that the words belong to a story. A different idea says a work of fiction acts like a prop in a game of make-believe: it guides readers about what to imagine. None of these ideas solves every case. Some histories are written in a lively way, and some fictional stories use real facts. This makes the boundary difficult. Philosophers also ask what is true in a story. “The hero lives in a castle” may be true in the story even if no such hero exists in our world. They ask how we decide what the story includes, especially when a narrator is unreliable or when the story contains contradictions. Another puzzle concerns feelings. We may pity or fear a character while knowing the character is not real. Some philosophers say these are special make-believe feelings; others say real emotions do not always require belief that their objects exist. Fiction may also help us learn facts, understand possibilities, or notice moral and emotional situations, although it can sometimes mislead us.
key_ideas: Fiction is not limited to books. Films, pictures, plays, and other representations can be fictional too.
A story can contain real facts and made-up parts at the same time.
Philosophers disagree about what makes something fiction: the writer’s purpose, the audience’s imagining, or features of the work.
We often respond emotionally to fictional characters, which raises questions about how those emotions work.
summaries.why_it_matters: Stories are not just entertainment. They help people imagine possibilities, understand characters, and think about truth, knowledge, and emotion. Studying fiction can also help us notice the difference between believing something and imagining it. That difference matters when we read novels, watch films, or decide whether a claim is meant as fact or as part of a story.

important_terms.definition: A story, picture, film, or other work that invites us to imagine people, events, or places, whether or not they are real.
Using imagination to treat something as if it were true for a game, story, or other activity.
A statement that is true inside a story, even when it is not true in the real world.
The puzzle of feeling emotions about a character we know does not really exist.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a story different from a newspaper report?
Can a fictional story teach you something true?
Why might you feel worried for a character you know is imaginary?

summaries.example: Consider a historical novel that portrays a real ruler and accurately describes a war, but invents private conversations. It is not simply non-fiction because the author does not present every scene as a factual record. Yet it is not wholly detached from truth: its setting may depend on accurate history, and its invented material may be used to explore political or moral possibilities. This case challenges definitions that identify fiction only with falsehood, invention, or pretense.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of fiction examines how fictional representation differs from truth-directed representation, how fictional truths work, what readers can learn, and how emotional engagement is possible. A simple semantic account defines fiction as falsehood or nonreference, but this is inadequate: textbooks can contain errors, fiction can accidentally describe reality accurately, and historical fiction often depends on substantial factual accuracy. More sophisticated theories focus on authorial invention, communicative intention, or special speech acts. Pretense accounts hold that an author presents content without undertaking the ordinary commitment to assert it as fact. Make-believe theories instead emphasize the audience: a work functions as a prop that prescribes imaginings. The disagreement is partly about whether fiction is fundamentally a feature of acts, works, statements, narratives, or genres. Difficult borderline cases include vivid histories, literary journalism, metaphors, and works containing both assertion and invention. The notion of truth in fiction introduces another problem. A sentence can be true in a story without being true of the actual world, and fictional truth often depends on implications, background assumptions, genre conventions, and interpretive practices rather than explicit wording alone. Lewis analyzes this using possible worlds and counterfactual comparison; Walton analyzes it through rules governing make-believe; other views appeal to fictional authors, real authors, or reader-oriented norms. Unreliable narrators and impossible or inconsistent stories expose limitations in each approach. key_ideas: Semantic definitions identify fiction with falsity or nonreference, but these fail because fiction can be wholly true and non-fiction can contain errors or invented material.

Author-centered theories emphasize invention or communicative intention. Pretense accounts explain why fabricated journalism need not count as fiction if it is presented as fact, but pretense alone can also occur in irony or mimicry.

Walton’s make-believe theory gives readers a central role: works prescribe imaginings. Critics argue that this may classify vivid histories, metaphors, or natural objects as fiction in an overly broad sense.
Accounts of truth in fiction must handle implication, background knowledge, genre conventions, unreliable narrators, and the difference between possible and impossible stories.
Fiction can communicate factual or deeper human understanding, but philosophers disagree about whether such knowledge is central to literary value and whether readers can reliably gain it.

The paradox of fiction is addressed by rejecting different parts of the puzzle: some deny that the response is an ordinary emotion, some change its object, and others deny that belief in existence is required for emotion.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fiction is a useful philosophical test case because it connects language, imagination, emotion, knowledge, and metaphysics. Understanding it clarifies why “true in a story” is not the same as “true in reality,” why authorial intention may matter without settling every interpretation, and why imagining a proposition differs from believing it. These distinctions also matter beyond literature: fictionalist approaches have been proposed in areas such as mathematics and morality, where some people recommend treating claims as useful without accepting their literal commitments.

important_terms.definition: A representation whose status as fiction is disputed or explained through features such as invention, authorial intention, audience response, and genre conventions.
A philosophical account that treats fiction-making as an author’s pretending to perform ordinary speech acts such as assertion.
The view that a representational work functions as a prop in a socially organized game that directs participants’ imaginings.
A statement that holds within a story’s represented setting, even though the statement may be false or indeterminate in the actual world.
The philosophical problem of how a work can determine truths when its story contains contradictions or impossible situations.
The view that fiction can contribute to knowledge, including factual, moral, conceptual, or practical understanding.
The puzzle that readers appear to feel emotions toward nonexistent characters while knowing that those characters do not exist.
A way of classifying works by features that are usual or unusual for the genre, rather than by strict necessary and sufficient conditions.

questions_to_think_about: Should a work’s classification depend more on the author’s intention, the reader’s response, or the work’s genre and context?
Can a historical novel be fictional even when many of its statements are true? What would make its truth accidental or intentional?
How should we interpret a story that says both that a character has a property and that the character lacks it?
Does reading a novel give knowledge, or does it mainly give a model of how a situation might appear to someone?
Are pity and fear directed at fictional characters, at the work itself, or at imagined situations?

summaries.example: Suppose your class reads a mystery about a missing school trophy. The story never says that the detective has a heartbeat, but you naturally assume it. It does say the detective found the trophy in the art room, so that is clearly true in the story. Now imagine that the writer accidentally describes the trophy as both silver and gold. Readers must decide whether one description is a mistake, whether the narrator is unreliable, or whether the story allows a contradiction. Philosophers study how such decisions work.
summaries.summary: People use fiction in books, films, pictures, plays, and many other forms. Philosophers ask what makes a work fictional rather than non-fictional. Defining fiction as false writing does not work, because a science book can contain errors and a fictional story can accidentally describe real events accurately. Defining it as non-reference also fails, because fiction can discuss real places and people. Some theories therefore emphasize the author’s creative activity or intention. On a pretense account, the author appears to make ordinary factual claims but does not intend readers to take the work as a literal report. On a make-believe account, the important point is that the work guides readers’ imagining, like a prop in a game. Critics object that this may make vivid histories or metaphors count as fiction. Other theories treat fiction and non-fiction as broad genres whose usual features can have exceptions. Philosophers also study fictional truth. A statement such as “the detective lives above the bakery” may be true in a story even though the detective is not a real person. Such truth can depend on explicit details, reasonable inferences, shared background beliefs, and genre rules. Problems arise with unreliable narrators, conflicting details, and stories that describe impossible events. Fiction may help readers gain factual, moral, psychological, or practical understanding, but some philosophers doubt that literary works provide knowledge or that knowledge is part of literary value. Finally, the paradox of fiction asks how readers can pity or fear fictional characters while knowing they do not exist. Proposed answers differ about belief, imagination, and the target of the emotion.
key_ideas: Calling something fiction is not the same as calling it false. A fictional work can include accurate facts, and a non-fiction work can contain mistakes.
Some philosophers focus on what authors do: invent material, pretend to assert it, or invite readers to imagine it in a particular way.
Other philosophers focus on readers and works. A text may function as a guide or prop for make-believe, although this view can classify some lively non-fiction as fiction.
A story can make claims true inside its own setting. These truths may come from what is stated, what follows from it, background knowledge, or genre expectations.
Philosophers disagree about whether fiction can give us knowledge, especially moral or practical knowledge. Readers may learn, but they can also be misled.
Our emotional responses to stories are real experiences, but philosophers disagree about whether they are ordinary emotions and what their objects are.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about fiction helps us understand how imagination differs from belief and how language can work in more than one way. It also helps us read carefully. We can ask whether a statement is meant as a fact, an invitation to imagine, a joke, or part of a story. Fiction matters because it can shape feelings, ideas, and views of possible situations, even while it raises questions about whether what we learn from it is reliable.

important_terms.definition: A made-up or imagined story, picture, film, play, or other representation that is treated differently from an ordinary report of facts.
The difference between what a work asks us to imagine and what a work presents as a report about the actual world.
An action performed with words, such as promising, asking, reporting, or pretending to report.
The act of presenting words as if one were making a normal factual claim, without taking on the same factual commitment.
A guided activity in which an object or text helps people imagine that certain things are happening.
Something that is the case according to a story, even if it is not the case in real life.
A narrator whose presentation cannot be accepted straightforwardly as a reliable guide to what is true in the story.
The problem of having feelings for fictional people even though we know those people are not real.

questions_to_think_about: If a writer invents a story but labels it a true report, should we call it fiction? Why or why not?
What unstated facts do you automatically add when reading a story?
Can a story be fiction even if every event in it happens to be true?
Why might a horror film make you feel afraid without making you run away?
What could a fictional story teach that a list of facts might not?
